question: For a simple undirected graph with N vertices given by its adjacency matrix A: (1) what does the entry (A^k)_{ij} represent, (2) how can one determine from A whether the graph is connected, and (3) what is the definition of a path between vertices n_i and n_j?

sources.title: Graph Theory (Grafneri tesutyun), course textbook in Armenian
sources.venue: Course textbook; publisher and year not read
sources.notes: Primary source for definitions and their numbers. Viewed as page images in this run (PDF page = printed page + 1; printed pages are cited): 9 (Def 1.1.1), 11 (Def 1.1.4, adjacency matrix), 12, 21 (Def 1.2.10), 22 (Defs 1.2.12, 1.2.13), 23 (distance properties, Lemma 1.2.1), 34, 48 (Def 2.1.1), 49, 61. Authors given by surname only, taken from the brief; first names, year and publisher were not read from a title page. Quotes are transcribed from the page images; the text layer drops symbols. Authors' word shrjantsum is rendered walk, chanaparh is the book's path (a trail, Def 1.2.12), partz chanaparh is simple path (Def 1.2.13), following graph-sources.md and the brief. A text-layer search for the adjacency-matrix phrase finds it only on printed pp. 7, 11, 12, 34, 61; p. 7 was not viewed as an image. No walk-counting theorem or matrix connectivity test was found on the pages viewed. Lemma 1.2.1 is stated for u different from v and has no length bound.

sources.title: Linear algebra notes, Chapter 1, 1.1 The Adjacency Matrix (University of Galway notes)
sources.notes: Opened and text-extracted in full (7 PDF pages; printed pages 2 to 8 by the footers, the section starts on printed p. 2). Carries no author name and no date; call them the University of Galway notes. Original teaching text with numbered statements, not peer reviewed. Defines simple undirected graph (Def 1.1.1, p. 2) and proves walk counting (Theorem 1.1.3, p. 4) by induction. Does not define walk or path. Marked partial because the later sections (spectral part, Friendship Theorem) were not read in detail. Math in the quotes is as flattened by text extraction (A^k appears as Ak).

sources.title: MIT 18.211 Combinatorial Analysis, Lecture 27: Adjacency Matrices and The Matrix-Tree Theorem
sources.notes: Opened; pages 1 and 2 read for Proposition 2 (walk counting, p. 1, graphs on [n], directed or undirected) and Proposition 3 (p. 2, the (I_n + A)^(n-1) form of the connectivity test for simple graphs). No date on the file. Proposition 3 is not the sum form A + ... + A^(n-1); its proof asserts the bound 'length at most n - 1' without proving it and uses a binomial identity. A footnote says Proposition 3 was not covered in class. Matrix-Tree part (pp. 2-4) not used. Math in quotes as flattened by text extraction.

sources.title: An introduction to graph theory (version June 7, 2025)
sources.notes: Downloaded the full PDF (454 pages) and read Section 2.9 (pp. 36-42) for simple graphs. Page numbers are the version's own (header 'page N'), which in this version equal the PDF page numbers. Original lecture text with numbered statements. Section 2.9 states the results for simple graphs; the multidigraph version of walk counting (Theorem 4.5.10, pp. 120-121) exists but was not needed. Rest of the book not read. Earlier runs recorded multidigraph-style statements for these results; in this version Section 2.9 is for simple graphs, and the page locators agree with graph-sources.md.

sources.title: Important Properties and Applications of the Adjacency Matrix (20250310)
sources.notes: Opened; Section 1 (pp. 1-2) read. Short lecture notes dated 2025-03-10 in the title. Defines walk and path (no repeated vertex), states walk counting as Theorem 1 for simple graphs and the (I + A)^(n-1) test as Theorem 2 with a proof sketch only. No sum form A + ... + A^(n-1). The proof sketch says '(I + A)^(n-1) aggregates all paths of length <= n - 1', which counts walks under the notes' own definition of path. Not peer reviewed. Eigenvalue sections not read.

sources.title: Properties of Adjacency Matrix of a Graph and It's Construction
sources.notes: Opened the full PDF (9 pages) and viewed page 17 as an image; pp. 13-17 read as text. Original research article in a faculty journal. The paper never defines 'path'. Theorem 1 (p. 16) says the entry of A^l counts 'different paths of length l'; Theorem 2 (p. 17) is the sum form of the test, B = A + ... + A^(n-1), and its proof moves from a non-zero entry to a path without a walk-to-path lemma; Theorem 3 (p. 17) is the distance statement. Quotes keep the printed wording; subscripts and superscripts are flattened to plain text.

sources.title: m1_walks.py: brute-force walk enumeration against matrix powers
sources.venue: Script written by module m1 in this run
sources.notes: Run with python3 -I; output saved in scripts/m1_walks_output.txt. Enumerates every vertex sequence of length k+1 and compares the count with the matrix power for the board matrix (k = 0..4) and for 200 random simple graphs on 2..6 vertices (k = 0..4). A check, not a proof.

sources.title: Undirected Graphs (COS 226 lecture slides)
sources.venue: Princeton University, COS 226 lecture slides (undirected.ppt as PDF)
sources.notes: Downloaded the PDF and extracted the text; read slide 24 (PDF p. 6) on depth-first search and its running time. The title-slide footer reads 'Robert Sedgewick and Kevin Wayne • Copyright © 2006 • http://www.Princeton.EDU/~cos226', which gives the authors and the year; the PDF metadata also names Kevin Wayne and a 2006 creation date. Slides, not peer reviewed. The slide is about depth-first search, not breadth-first search. The rest of the deck was not read.

sources.title: m2_connectivity_test.py: matrices, sums and walk lists for the sum test
sources.venue: Script written by module m2 in this run
sources.notes: Run with python3 -I; output saved in scripts/m2_connectivity_test.out. Computes A, its powers and S = A + ... + A^(N-1) for the board graph, a disconnected graph on 3 vertices and the path graph on 4 vertices, lists the walks that chosen entries count, compares each S_ij with a brute-force walk count and each verdict with a brute-force path search, and prints (I + A)^(N-1) for the board and disconnected graphs. A check of examples, not a proof.

contradictions.summary: The textbook's word 'path' (chanaparh, Definition 1.2.12) means a walk with distinct edges (a trail), and its Definition 2.1.1 of connected uses that word. The course's path (user's summary) and the paper's path is the textbook's simple path, Definition 1.2.13, a walk with no repeated vertex.
contradictions.resolution: The paper says in one clause where it defines path that it means Definition 1.2.13 and defines connected with that path. Trail-connected and path-connected agree because a walk contains a path (C24) and a path has distinct edges; the trail reading must be proved in the paper, Grinberg Proposition 2.9.10 covers walks and paths only.

contradictions.summary: Paramadevan and Sotheeswaran say A^l entries count 'different paths of length l'; the Galway notes, Gotti and Bai say walks, and Bai says explicitly not paths. The two agree only if 'path' in Paramadevan means walk, which the paper never says.
contradictions.resolution: The paper proves the walk statement and gives the board counterexample for the vertex-distinct reading; it records both readings of Paramadevan's undefined word (optional item O3).

contradictions.summary: Bai's Theorem 1 says matrix powers count walks and not paths, while the proof sketch of Theorem 2 says (I + A)^(n-1) aggregates all paths of length at most n - 1.
contradictions.resolution: Under Bai's own definition (no repeated vertex) the sketch is wrong as written for R_11 on the board graph; the paper proves the test through walks and does not use the sketch.

contradictions.summary: The textbook's Lemma 1.2.1 is stated for different vertices and has no length bound; Grinberg's Corollary 2.9.7 covers u = v and gives length at most k, with the bound n - 1 on p. 40.
contradictions.resolution: Not a disagreement about truth; the paper takes the lemma with the case u = v and the bound from Grinberg and proves them in the text.

contradictions.summary: Textbook Definition 2.1.1 uses the textbook's path (trail, Definition 1.2.12); the paper's path is Definition 1.2.13 (no repeated vertex).
contradictions.resolution: Settled in m1-4: the two readings of connected agree, by Proposition 1 in modules/m1.md. Direction 2 uses N6 from module m2.
